section_summary: This section is dominated by letters, postcards, resolutions, editorials, and newspaper clippings protesting continued American petroleum exports to Japan while Secretary of the Interior Harold L. Ickes advocated domestic gasoline conservation and possible “gasless Sundays.” Correspondents repeatedly characterize the policy as appeasement and hypocrisy, arguing that American oil enabled Japan’s war in China and might later be used against the United States, Britain, or the Netherlands East Indies. The section also documents particular tanker shipments, the strategic importance of American and Dutch oil to Japan, Standard Oil’s defense of its trade, and demands for a complete embargo.

subfiles.title: Isidor Shaffer to President Roosevelt protesting appeasement of Japan
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt; copy to Harold L. Ickes
subfiles.about: Shaffer urges the administration to stop supplying Japan and other Axis-aligned powers with strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Isidor Shaffer cites Japan's imminent move into French Indochina as proof appeasement has failed and demands the U.S. stop supplying weapons and supplies.

subfiles.title: Chicago letter opposing gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The writer challenges proposals for gasless Sundays while American gasoline and scrap metal continue going to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chicago letter contrasts conservation appeals with about a million barrels of gasoline monthly to Japan and asks Ickes to stop the trade.

subfiles.title: Jack Hess on the futility of voluntary gasoline conservation
subfiles.about: Hess warns that the public will not conserve gasoline voluntarily while petroleum is exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jack Hess, an administration supporter, calls the conservation campaign futile under current export policy, saying publicized shipments to Japan damage credibility.

subfiles.title: Woman’s Club of Jacksonville request for an explanation
subfiles.from: Mrs. Horace C. Avery, Woman’s Club of Jacksonville
subfiles.about: Avery asks why Americans are solicited to aid China while their government permits oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jacksonville Woman's Club, 750 members, calls aid to China alongside oil sales to Japan an appalling inconsistency; some women withhold Chinese relief gifts.

subfiles.title: Robert A. Hume protest over bombing of Chungking
subfiles.about: Hume refuses to conserve gasoline while American oil enables Japanese bombing attacks on Chongqing.
subfiles.summary: Robert Hume angrily asks whether he must deny himself gasoline so the bombing of Chongqing can continue.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Caldwell on oil conservation and wildlife protection
subfiles.about: Caldwell suggests stopping oil shipments to Japan as the most effective conservation measure.
subfiles.summary: Robert Caldwell says conserving oil requires ending sales to Japan, and also urges closing the hunting season to protect the wood duck.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Donald D. Van Slyke on unequal conservation demands
subfiles.about: Van Slyke asks how citizens can be expected to conserve fuel while the government permits large gasoline sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter quotes the complaint that consumers are not falling into line quickly enough with voluntary fuel conservation. Van Slyke replies that restrictions on Americans are unreasonable while roughly a million barrels can be exported to an aggressor.

subfiles.title: R. E. Huddleston protest over Pacific Coast gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Huddleston links prospective gasless Sundays to continuing gasoline exports from the Pacific Coast to Japan.
subfiles.summary: R. E. Huddleston reports a large gasoline shipment leaving the Pacific Coast for Japan and asks why Ickes doesn't act before restricting Sunday driving.

subfiles.title: Village Inn forwarding item on excessive gasoline use
subfiles.from: Unknown correspondent at the Village Inn
subfiles.about: A fragmentary item forwards a clipping about enforcement against excessive gasoline consumption.
subfiles.summary: Village Inn letterhead with a clipping on police finding fifty excessive gasoline users; any message is illegible.

subfiles.title: A. M. Berson appeal to stop oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Berson condemns American oil shipments that fuel Japanese air raids in China.
subfiles.summary: A. M. Berson, citing photographs of Japanese destruction, asks whether the U.S. will keep aiding attacks on China and calls for an immediate halt to shipments.

subfiles.title: Reed C. Rollins note on Japanese tanker loading
subfiles.about: Rollins forwards or cites a report that the Kokuyo Maru was loading oil for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Damaged note from Reed Rollins on a Japanese tanker loading about 140,000 barrels, questioning consistency with conservation demands.

subfiles.title: Jean C. Reid request for an explanation of tanker exports
subfiles.about: Reid asks why large quantities of oil are leaving the country for a belligerent nation.
subfiles.summary: Jean Reid sends a clipping listing cargoes for the Iro, Tonan Maru III and Kyokuyo Maru and asks why oil goes to a belligerent while Americans conserve.

subfiles.title: Paul St.-Gaudens on the credibility of gasoline conservation
subfiles.about: St.-Gaudens says the gasoline campaign cannot succeed while the government permits oil sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Paul St.-Gaudens calls the conservation policy hypocritical because American fuel supports an Axis partner's war on China; people ask why save gasoline to send to Japan.

subfiles.title: Norfolk protest over domestic conservation and foreign oil sales
subfiles.about: The writer questions demands for fuel conservation while hundreds of thousands of barrels are exported.
subfiles.summary: Norfolk letter, largely illegible, contrasts fuel-saving appeals with a reported shipment of about 400,000 barrels and asks how the policies are justified.

subfiles.title: Albert Strauss demand to stop shipments before asking sacrifice
subfiles.about: Strauss says he will accept personal gasoline sacrifices only after shipments to Japan are stopped.
subfiles.summary: Albert Strauss says limiting gasoline for defense is no great burden, but insists Ickes stop Japanese shipments first.

subfiles.title: Clippings on Japanese oil cargoes and Ickes’s conservation appeal
subfiles.about: Juxtaposed clippings report large Japanese tanker cargoes and Ickes’s appeal for a 20-percent reduction in Eastern petroleum consumption.
subfiles.summary: Clippings: over 400,000 barrels loading at San Pedro on the Kokuyo Maru, Iro, Tonan Maru III and Kyokuyo Maru; and Ickes's voluntary conservation program for sixteen Eastern states.

subfiles.title: J. J. Haight on four Japanese oil cargoes
subfiles.about: Haight contrasts a reported petroleum emergency with the loading of four tankers for Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. J. Haight reproduces a New York Sun report of over 400,000 barrels for Japanese ships at San Pedro and calls the exports indefensible given Japan's alliance with Germany.

subfiles.title: Harry E. Hatoff letter with Boston Globe oil clipping
subfiles.about: Hatoff condemns a policy that opposes aggression while supplying Japan with the means to wage it.
subfiles.summary: Harry Hatoff attaches a Boston Globe report of over 400,000 barrels shipped from Los Angeles Harbor, saying the U.S. fights aggressors while strengthening them.

subfiles.title: Archie Fine appeal for China and world goodwill
subfiles.about: Fine argues that American sales to Japan inflict an irreparable wrong on China.
subfiles.summary: The partially illegible letter portrays the United States as a Christian nation responsible for aiding an aggressor’s destruction of China. Fine warns that if China collapses, Americans must accept a share of the blame and asks who now controls national policy.

subfiles.title: Illegible handwritten appeal to Harold Ickes
subfiles.about: A largely illegible correspondent appears to protest American assistance connected with the war in China.
subfiles.summary: Illegible handwritten appeal to Harold Ickes, apparently about Japan, China and American war materials.

subfiles.title: Blacksmiths’ helpers union resolution against oil exports
subfiles.from: Bob Fisher, secretary, blacksmiths’ helpers union
subfiles.about: A union membership demands that shipments to Japan cease before citizens are asked to curtail gasoline use.
subfiles.summary: Blacksmiths' helpers union says conservation demands are premature while exports continue, with oil bombing China and possibly turned on the U.S.

subfiles.title: W. Arthur Faus on gasless Sundays and church attendance
subfiles.about: Faus opposes domestic fuel restrictions while oil is sold to Germany and Japan and asks that church travel be protected from Sunday limits.
subfiles.summary: Minister W. Arthur Faus says Americans accept reasonable sacrifices but not while oil firms supply aggressors, and warns Sunday driving bans would hurt rural church attendance.

subfiles.title: Anonymous West New York letter attacking the gasless-Sunday campaign
subfiles.about: The writer criticizes conservation publicity while fuel continues to be exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The damaged four-page letter asks why the United States has exported fuel to Japan and refers to tankers loading near Hoboken. It mocks publicity about gasless Sundays and “jackrabbit” driving, and recommends preserving fuel for Americans instead.

subfiles.title: Henry Phillips Jr. on State Department oil policy
subfiles.about: Phillips argues that conservation will gain support only when the State Department resolves its policy toward oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Henry Phillips Jr. backs aid to Britain but sees no reason to sustain Japan's military, urges Ickes to stop exports from both coasts, and alleges appeasers in the State Department.

subfiles.title: G. Blake’s bicycle request for gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: Blake sarcastically asks where to rent a bicycle in order to watch tankers load American oil for Japan.
subfiles.summary: G. Blake satirically asks for a bicycle for gasless Sundays, to ride from Oakland to Richmond and watch tankers load fuel for Japan.

subfiles.title: Anonymous Auburn letter on the Scheherazade affair and State Department appeasement
subfiles.about: An admirer of Ickes asks him to oppose the Scheherazade oil delivery and forward the protest to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Anonymous Auburn letter praises Ickes on helium, a Japanese tanker and Lindbergh, but says the Scheherazade affair favored Vichy, weakened Britain and disrupted the Anglo-American-Dutch posture toward Japan.

subfiles.title: Ethel Tuttle on conserving gasoline for Japan
subfiles.about: Tuttle says Americans cannot be persuaded to save gasoline while their government permits supplies to reach Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer asks why Japanese needs are placed above American needs and questions whether Ickes lacks authority or refuses to use it. She concludes that an official who insists on domestic conservation while facilitating Japanese aggression against China should be removed from office.

subfiles.title: Note forwarding a New York Post item
subfiles.about: The writer forwards a July 10 New York Post item that acquaintances found difficult to understand.
subfiles.summary: Note forwarding a New York Post item that confused several people, on conservation versus oil exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Darien correspondent on appeasement and oil conservation
subfiles.about: The writer says conservation cooperation is impossible while large fuel quantities are shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter argues that any shortage provides a reason to stop Japanese shipments and directs Ickes to explain the policy to the nation. It calls appeasement of Japan wrong and says exports should have ceased long before.

subfiles.title: Eaton M. MacKay on Pacific Coast tanker loadings
subfiles.about: MacKay protests continuing Pacific Coast oil shipments after reports that an embargo was avoided to deter Japanese expansion into southern Asia.
subfiles.summary: Eaton MacKay says Californians see appeasing Japan as a concession to oil companies, asks whether withholding an embargo restrained Japan, and urges an end to "pussy-footing."

subfiles.title: Washington state legislator requests facts on oil policy
subfiles.about: A state legislator forwards an Elma Chronicle editorial and asks for an explanation of oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Washington state legislator says an oil company blamed the administration's policy, fears war with Japan, and asks Ickes for the facts.

subfiles.title: Lumpkin Lions Club resolution against aid to Axis associates
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt; copies to federal and Georgia officials
subfiles.about: The club calls for a permanent end to oil and other aid to Japan, Vichy France, and allies or associates of Hitler.
subfiles.summary: The cover letter reports unanimous adoption of the enclosed resolution. The resolution deplores oil sales to Japan, assistance to Vichy France, and the unfreezing of relevant assets, while opposing any munitions, appeasement, aid, or comfort for the friends of aggression.

subfiles.title: Long Beach letter with Toei Maru clipping
subfiles.about: The correspondent cites the loading of the Toei Maru as a reason gasless Sundays will lack public support.
subfiles.summary: Long Beach letter with a clipping on the Toei Maru loading oil at Standard Oil's Berth 101, asking how Ickes can promote gasless Sundays meanwhile.

subfiles.title: Charles J. Everett appeal to stop oil sales
subfiles.about: Everett urges Ickes to end oil shipments to Japan unless compelling facts unknown to the public justify them.
subfiles.summary: Charles Everett asks a halt to petroleum exports, noting similar messages to other cabinet officials, apparently Knox and Stimson.

subfiles.title: Cleveland forwarding pages including “Oil Still Flows Freely to Japan”
subfiles.about: Forwarded newspaper pages document defense news and list tanker shipments carrying more than 1.25 million barrels from San Pedro.
subfiles.summary: The relevant article says Japan could lose more than a million barrels per month if its cabinet adopted a pro-Axis course. It itemizes fourteen June and July tanker departures from San Pedro, identifies the Iro and Kokuyo as naval tankers, and notes additional petroleum moving as dry cargo.

subfiles.title: James Tooker Ford on the western oil-export contradiction
subfiles.about: Ford attacks the inconsistency of restricting Eastern oil use while permitting western exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: James Ford calls lending China money while supplying Japan hypocritical, cites Standard Oil testimony, and asks whether the government is subservient to the company.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Simeon J. Hardy thanks Ickes for halting a shipment
subfiles.about: Hardy expresses approval of Ickes’s reported action halting an oil shipment and hopes the government will cease aiding Japan against China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Simeon Hardy thanks Ickes for halting a shipment and urges continued efforts to deny Japan materials used to destroy China.

subfiles.title: Arthur N. Bean praises Ickes and urges an end to oil shipments
subfiles.about: Bean praises Ickes’s Connecticut speech and asks him to defend America and its allies by stopping oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Minister Arthur Bean praises Ickes's forceful speech, urges aid to Britain, and insists Germany and Japan must not receive materials able to destroy civilization.

subfiles.title: Clippings calling for a petroleum ban on Japan
subfiles.from: Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies; unidentified newspaper
subfiles.to: Newspaper readers and the State Department
subfiles.about: The clippings pair Ickes’s conservation warning with a committee demand that petroleum export licenses for Japan be denied.
subfiles.summary: Clippings: a committee reports gasoline exports to Japan rose 280 percent over 1940 and warns oil supports the China war and possible expansion toward Singapore and the East Indies.

subfiles.title: “U.S. Still Provides 60% of Oil Used by Japan’s War Machine”
subfiles.about: The article analyzes Japan’s dependence on American and Netherlands East Indies petroleum and the strategic consequences of an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Article estimates the U.S. supplies over 60 percent of Japan's oil, with lower-octane and west-coast shipments blunting restrictions; an embargo could provoke an attempt on Dutch oil fields, a dangerous gamble.

subfiles.title: July 15 handwritten protest to Ickes
subfiles.about: The writer questions restrictions on New York-area oil use while exports continue elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: Poorly legible July 15 protest to Ickes on the unequal burden on New York consumers while Japanese shipments continue.

subfiles.title: Photographic feature on the Chungking air-raid shelter disaster
subfiles.about: The feature presents photographs of victims of the June 6 suffocation disaster in a Chongqing air-raid shelter.
subfiles.summary: Photo feature: about 700 Chinese civilians died in the Chungking air-raid shelter disaster after ventilation failed.

subfiles.title: Associated Press clipping on four Japanese oil cargoes
subfiles.about: The report describes four vessels taking more than 400,000 barrels of oil from Los Angeles Harbor.
subfiles.summary: Associated Press clipping: the Kokuyo Maru and Iro were loading 70,000 and 54,000 barrels, with the Tonan Maru III and Kyokuyo Maru to sail with 140,000 each.

subfiles.title: Oil-shipment clipping with handwritten comparison to British arms sales
subfiles.about: An annotator compares American oil exports to Japan with earlier British munitions sales to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Clipping of over 400,000 barrels for Japanese vessels at San Pedro, with a handwritten warning against Britain's shortsightedness when purchased munitions returned as shrapnel.

subfiles.title: Postcard addressed to Secretary Ickes
subfiles.about: The surviving page is the address side of a postcard sent to Ickes.
subfiles.summary: Postcard addressed to Secretary Ickes with no legible message, presumably about petroleum shipments.

subfiles.title: Pharr editorial opposing gasless Sundays while oil goes to Japan
subfiles.about: The editorial says Americans will not accept gasoline rationing while the government authorizes large petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editor argues that U.S. aid to China is nullified by supplying Japan and predicts that a firm embargo could force peace within six months. The page continues with commentary on Iceland, Germany, and American passivity, alongside unrelated local reporting about salaries, charitable sewing, and hunting regulations.

subfiles.title: Anonymous submission of “Latest Bulletin on ‘Gas’-Less Sundays”
subfiles.about: An anonymous sender forwards a sarcastically captioned report on Japanese oil loading at San Pedro.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reports that Japanese vessels were taking more than 400,000 barrels from Los Angeles Harbor. Its “latest bulletin” heading presents the shipment as a direct rebuttal to proposals for gasless Sundays.

subfiles.title: Anonymous annotated clipping, “Oil from U.S. for Japan”
subfiles.about: The annotation asks whether Japanese users should enjoy Sunday fuel while Americans face an alleged shortage.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reports tanker loadings at Los Angeles Harbor, including the Kokuyo Maru, Iro, and Tonan Maru III. The sender’s handwritten questions suggest that the oil may eventually return to the United States in the form of hostile military force.

subfiles.title: Anonymous editorials demanding an Axis blacklist and Japanese oil embargo
subfiles.to: Harold L. Ickes and newspaper readers
subfiles.about: The editorials argue that any blacklist of Axis suppliers should begin with an embargo on oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: “Yes, Let’s Blacklist the Axis” calls Japan the Far Eastern branch of the Axis and accuses Washington of urging companies to supply it while Americans conserve. A second clipping supplies the immediate example: more than 400,000 barrels being loaded at San Pedro.

subfiles.title: Cover letter and New Haven clippings on conservation and foreign trade
subfiles.about: The sender requests an explanation of domestic petroleum reductions and encloses newspaper material on gasoline conservation and Japanese trade.
subfiles.summary: The New Haven clippings contrast Ickes’s appeal for a 20-percent Eastern reduction with Japanese receipt of more than 400,000 barrels from Los Angeles Harbor. Additional material describes Japan’s shipment of foodstuffs to Germany, its search for metals, and its oil arrangements in the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: “Veritas” letter criticizing preferential shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: The writer asks why American citizens face restrictions while shipments continue to a potential enemy.
subfiles.summary: Fragment of a "Veritas" letter blaming poor planning and discrimination in Japan's favor and calling for an immediate halt to exports.

subfiles.title: Vallejo letter to the editor supporting an anti-oil editorial
subfiles.about: The writer praises an editorial opposing oil, gasoline, and scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vallejo letter to the editor calls conservation ridiculous while Japan allies with Germany, criticizes administration contradictions, cites Senator Wheeler, and endorses humanitarian aid and church peace mediation.

subfiles.title: “The Gasoline Situation Seems Inconsistent to Us”
subfiles.about: The editorial supports national defense but criticizes domestic rationing while Japanese tankers load oil in Suisun Bay.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "The Gasoline Situation Seems Inconsistent to Us" grants Eastern transport shortages but says motorists shouldn't sacrifice; it urges reserving oil for the U.S. and allies and treating Japan like its Axis partners.

subfiles.title: Illustrated article on Japanese purchases of American war materials
subfiles.about: The article documents American oil, metals, scrap, and cotton exports used by Japan’s war machine.
subfiles.summary: Article: controls on high-octane gasoline and scrap left many petroleum products available to Japan; it compares 1939 and 1940 exports, and Representatives Coffee and Anderson demand stronger investigation.

subfiles.title: Akron Beacon Journal editorial and cartoon, “Plug That Leak, Harold”
subfiles.from: Akron Beacon Journal; forwarded by Fred C. Theifs
subfiles.about: The editorial urges Ickes to stop petroleum exports before imposing gasless Sundays on Americans.
subfiles.summary: It reviews American sales of petroleum, machine tools, and raw materials to Japan and notes a 50-percent year-on-year increase in March petroleum exports. A cartoon depicts Japan seeking gasoline from a dwindling American supply, while the editorial calls an embargo Ickes’s first duty as petroleum administrator.

subfiles.title: Note endorsing a “Gas-less Sundays Coming for U.S.” cartoon
subfiles.about: The writer tells Ickes that a cartoon about impending gasless Sundays speaks for the public.
subfiles.summary: Brief handwritten endorsement of a "Gas-less Sundays Coming for U.S." cartoon protesting conservation amid exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Newspaper page on an Eastern oil shortage and gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: The page reports Ickes’s response to an Eastern transportation shortage and juxtaposes it with protests about oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ickes says the Eastern oil problem is inadequate tankers and pipelines, not supply, and considers voluntary gasless Sundays and less winter heating; commentary asks why Americans face limits while oil goes to a potential enemy.

subfiles.title: “Standard to Keep Sending Oil to Japs”
subfiles.about: The article reports Standard Oil’s defense of an agreement to sell additional ordinary petroleum products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: "Standard to Keep Sending Oil to Japs": W. S. Farish says Standard-Vacuum's agreement was made with the American, British and East Indies governments' knowledge and normal trade continues until U.S. policy changes.

subfiles.title: “Gasless Sundays and Less Heat in Homes Proposed”
subfiles.about: The report warns the Eastern United States to expect less gasoline and heating oil beginning July 1.
subfiles.summary: AP: petroleum experts recommend gasless Sundays and lower home temperatures to prevent shortages hurting defense production; an industry committee reports to Ickes and pledges cooperation.

subfiles.title: “This Fast Life” editorial condemning oil sales through the local harbor
subfiles.about: The column calls continued oil exports to Japan inexcusable while Ickes warns of gasless Sundays in the East.
subfiles.summary: "This Fast Life" column blames the government but says exporting firms know the military destination, mentions a growing boycott, and predicts public opposition will end the trade.

subfiles.title: Letter criticizing aid to Vichy and cartoon on gasless Sundays for Japan
subfiles.doc_type: letter to the editor and cartoon
subfiles.about: The final items criticize State Department accommodation of Vichy France and satirize unequal gasoline restrictions favoring Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. K. R. argues that food cargoes to Vichy strengthen fascist and Nazi leadership rather than democracy and calls for more courageous State Department officials. The accompanying cartoon’s surviving caption contrasts American Sunday restrictions with the absence of “gasless Sundays” for Japan.
